entry.title: Link Blog 3
entry.content:
• I can waste hours looking at things like this Interactive World History Atlas since 3000 BC.
  • The BBC’s In Our Time is one of the best podcasts available. Although with around 30 years of old episodes it can be hard to find the one you are interested in (especially through RSS). Fear not, the Explore the In Our Time archive has you covered.
  • Why Is Venus Hell and Earth an Eden?. As the title suggests.
  • Learn X in Y minutes is a handy reminder tool for the syntax and basic control of most languages. I’ve already found it useful when needing to code in a long forgotten (by me) language.
  • Send this article to your friend who still thinks the cloud is a good idea. Interesting calculation of cloud vs hosted costs of an online service. I’ve always done the later.
  • BALL x PIT: My game of the year 2025 is a mildly interesting article about what the writer thinks BALL x PIT does right. I haven’t played the game, so can’t comment on that. What I found super interesting was a small point made near the end - the “Easy, Hard, Easy” loops in popular games on Steam. Damn, when I read that, it was a revelation. I have felt it as a player but not conceptualised it as a developer. Definitely something I will look to include in my games.
  • Internet security and avoiding ads (know that the two are intrinsically linked!) is important. How I block all online ads & An easy-to-use digital safety checklist are good lists of things that can be done to help. I haven’t done all the things listed, but certainly have gone through more than the basics.

entry.title: Boardgames of 2025
entry.content:
Last year I played less boardgames than 2024. Mostly this is due to not playing online and just being busy with other things (travel, etc) so missing game days. I expect to play more this year. I have started playing with a couple of groups more regularly. The 6 train games on the list were played at the 18XX group. For more information on why these games are worth playing checkout this post. The miniature wargames played this year (Strength & Honour and Armada) are with a friend from the local strategy boardgame group who turned out to live nearby and enjoy such games (a lucky find!).

The full list of this year’s games is below, with the ones I own in italics.

Game Plays
Splendor Duel 9
Strength & Honour 4
Star Wars Armada 3
Hissy Fit 3
Undaunted: Normandy 2
1846 2
Molly House 2
Wingspan 2
Agamemnon 2
1844/1854 1
1830 1
18Chesapeake 1
Star Trek: Frontiers 1
Red Dust Rebellion 1
Burning Banners 1
Fire in the Lake 1
Age of Steam 1
Chicago Express 1
Fate of the Fellowship 1
Limit 1

Here are my thoughts on some games I played multiple times this year, and haven’t previously reviewed:

  • Splendor Duel: A two-player version of the popular Splendor. Collect gems to create jewellery and thus your fortune. Not sure I’m qualified to discuss this one due to a very low win ratio. I must be missing something which suggests a relatively and surprisingly deep game for the simple mechanics. Still a fun quick game, will play again.
  • Strength & Honour: A 2mm scale ancients miniatures wargame, although we played successfully with just pieces of cardboard. Victories are won by forcing your enemy to break, but sometimes you just can’t get your units to act. Initial placement of units and maintaining a supporting line are vital. Very interesting and will play more as we are going through linked scenarios designed by my opponent.
  • Star Wars Armada: Amazingly pretty miniatures wargame of Star Wars capital ship battles. The fighting seems to be based on naval battles with large slow moving ships pummeling each other while small squadrons nibble around the edges. Satisfying game that seems mostly decided by the meta-game.
  • Undaunted: Normandy: Extremely clever deckbuilder of WWII squad level combat. The cards in hand represent your ability to order squads to acts. You then play cards to move across a map created from various combinations of terrain tiles. The mechanics and theme fit very well. Hopefully will get to play this much more over the coming year.
  • Molly House: I played this at the Strategy Boardgames group and it took two plays to understand what was going on - I’d happily play a third. Feels like a very tactical game (well laid plans go astray quickly) of “coopertition” - you have to both cooperate and compete with the fellow players. Like a mix of Churchill and a slightly less complex Pax Pamir. All this in a game about throwing gay parties and dodging police in 18th century London. Amazing.
  • Agamemnon: Supposedly a short game about the Trojan war, but is really an abstract area control game with the thinnest of themes applied over the top. Entertaining but forgettable.
  • Hissy Fit: A 5-minute party card game about getting a rowdy cat to the vet. Quick, easy and fun, but no need to play again.

entry.title: Goals 2026
entry.content:
So how did I go with last year’s goals?

  • Return to a decent level of fitness and strength: Partial success. I have started indoor cycling and my aerobic fitness is improving. However, I have barely gone to the gym at all this year.
  • Improve Spanish: Achieved, at least as far as practicing almost every day. I think I am better, but can’t be certain.
  • Start Ci2D: Started, but barely. So far it’s just a proof that Godot can meet my needs.
  • Modelling for 3D printing: Nope, nothing. Also seems less important now. I have too many unprinted models and a large grey pile of shame. There is no need to create more.
  • Read books: Achieved. The goal was met with a fortnight to go, and I made it explicitly because there was a target to reach. I have read some good books this year, and a couple that were not for me, but enjoyed the process of reading all of them. I will definitely try this again.

For the coming year I’ve decided to be more specific and less ambitious in my goals (following the success of last year’s Read books goal). I don’t want achieving a goal to be a struggle, and I want measurable results. They should be a starting point for a better life. The more aspirational or vague things I would like to do are now in a separate list. I won’t feel bad if I don’t even start them.

Goals:

  • Read 12 books: Worked well last year, let’s try it again.
  • Read social media less than 10 minutes/day on 300+ days: I have found myself spending increasing amounts of time on various sorts of social media. I would set this to 0, but unfortunately some groups and people are only contactable through these platforms. So 10 minutes should be more than enough to discover/organise with them. This limit also includes YouTube shorts/clips. It does not include news, but not sure what to do with the overlap (as much of modern news output is dross). I’ll have to work that out. I already had 2 days this year (out of 5!) where I exceeded this limit, so will have to improve.
  • 105 exercise sessions: At this time the main thing is just to keep exercising regularly. This is 2 sessions/week, enough to keep momentum. A bit more and there should be improvement.
  • Practice Spanish for 10+ minutes/day: About what I already do. As part of this I should try moving away from Duolingo, I am find the gains there slowing. I need to practice listening and grammar drills more than that site allows (on their free program).

Aspirations:

  • Sit Less: At the start of last year my desk chair broke and I replaced it with an ergonomic office chair. It works, too well! Now I sit a lot more and for longer. There is a correlation between sitting for extended periods and my back aching or legs being stiff. I should make better use of my sit/stand desk, and limit sitting to 30 minutes or so at a time.
  • Learn Python; try AI coding; general programming: Just code for fun.
  • Paint gray pile of shame: Painting minis takes much longer than I expected. It is very easy to print faster than I can paint, and so now I have 10+ Armada, 10+ X-wing, and nearly 100 Battletech minis waiting for paint, plus lots of tokens and terrain. I should work through it as much as possible (not all of it, realistically there is more than a year’s worth there).
  • CI2D demo: Rather than create full games, I will now aim to create demos, and see later which ones are worth pursuing.
  • Catch up on old blog threads: There are a bunch of notes for blog posts yet to be written. I haven’t written about my time in KL or Valencia. My work history series stops in 2005. These should be continued before the memory fades (if that hasn’t happened already).
  • Start learning Mandarin: I started learning Mandarin this year for a few weeks on Duolingo, but then they changed the way the site worked so that it became unreasonably hard to do more than one course. So Mandarin was given up in favour of continuing Spanish.
  • Play 5 boardgames at least 5 times: Almost made this in 2024 without trying. With a bit of attention it should be easy and fun. Online plays count.
entry.summary: So how did I go with last year’s goals?

entry.title: Somewhere Else
entry.content:
“I hope someone else tries it”, is something I think regularly with some of the less orthodox ideas suggested for government policy. Despite being interesting, they mostly they never happen anywhere but if they do I would prefer the first attempt to not be where I’m living. These are the kind of things that are unlikely to work due to unforeseen consequences, at least on first attempt. However, if they did work, could be hugely beneficial. For example, I hope someone tries a Universal Basic Income at the national level. However due to a large amount of cynicism, I would prefer Australia is not first.

Anyway, a social media ban for kids, I hope someone else tries it. Oh well.

entry.title: Bye
entry.content:
No, I’m not leaving, nor is this site. However some issues mean that my games will appear a bit less online.

The big issue is Itch.io. As of writing this, it has been 198 days since I initiated a payout for sales of my games (the first time I have done so on Itch), and it is still listed as “In Review”. The website says payouts should take 10-14 days. I created a support issue after 20 days and updated it after 34. After 50 days they said I need to update my tax information, which I did the same day (and let them know). Some weeks later the new tax info was listed as validated, but 100 days after that, still nothing has appeared.

I now have no trust in Itch.io. I have removed my games from sale there and they, nor any other game I control, will be available for sale there in the future (previously purchased copies will still accessible). Another addition to the “never again” company list.

At the same time I requested payouts from the other online stores I use. Humble paid out in their stated timeframe without issue - good for them! Steam had some problems with my company name (despite the exact same name being fine for the previous payout). I had to change it to my actual name and then the payout went through. Annoying, but forgivable given their support was prompt and helpful. Although a month later the listed name throughout their system was changed back to the original company name - strange.

There was a similar bureaucratic tax issue with the hosting provider for online Concealed Intent games. However, I found their support especially unhelpful. I don’t want to get into the specifics, but I was left wondering why I am paying these people (Linode, now a part of Akamai). Moving to another provider would be difficult, so I checked the state of the online server. There have been 2 connections to the server in the last 12 months. Two game requests in the last 3 years. The last actual online game was played in 2021! I’m thinking of shutting it down and so have removed mention of online play on the sales pages.

As part of this Concealed Intent is not going on sale for the foreseeable future. I expect this means sales will go to 0. So far so good, the last copy sold was during the last sale in March. It has been 10 years since the game was released, time to let it rest.

Update 1/1/2026: A copy of Concealed Intent was sold on Steam at full price (!) in November. Something that hasn’t happened for some time. Now I feel obliged to keep the servers running a little longer. Itch payout is still marked as “In Review”, so nothing changes there.
entry.summary: No, I’m not leaving, nor is this site. However some issues mean that my games will appear a bit less online.

entry.title: New Year, New Games
entry.content:
Games played since the start of 2025…

Inkulatini (5 hrs) - High concept 2D turn-based tactical strategy. The high concept? The player is drawing animals and monsters in the margins of a medieval manuscript, where they fight similar creatures. Sometimes a cute rabbit with a sword, or a donkey farting on the enemy, or many others. A very good idea and it carries the game through the otherwise standard gameplay. A fun little game, and you already know enough to know if you will like it too.

Starship Troopers: Terran Command (5 hrs) - Small unit RTS based on the movie based on the book. I seemed to spend far more time fighting the GUI & controls than the enemy. The mouse pointer was so small I often found myself searching for it in the heat of battle. Also my troopers seemed incredibly stupid, but maybe that is thematic. I wanted to like this game, but couldn’t.

Heretic’s Fork (10 hrs) - A deckbuilder crossed with tower defense (perhaps a liitle idle game influence too) where your job is punishing sinners trying to escape Hell. Nice idea, but the game is too slow. Even on max speed you spend most of the game watching your tower defense play out with nothing to do but wait. Also the UI needs some work - it is hard to see the status of the various variables the cards are manipulating (it is possible but awkward). Still this added enough interesting wrinkles to the deckbuilding formula to keep me entertained a few hours.

Griftlands (10 hrs) - This is a slickly produced game. Honestly, that is the first thing I noticed, just how well made it is. Griftlands is a deckbuilder battler set in a sci-fi world. To the standard Slay the Spire gameplay, it adds a story and a second type of card battle: negotiation. Both the additions work very well - I enjoyed playing it. However, I don’t feel a need to play more. Why? I’m not entirely sure, but my best guess is that the story and extra combat dilutes the fun of the core loop. A run takes several hours (over 4hrs to get to the end boss) and maybe that is just too long. It will stay on my drive for now and I’ll see if there is interest later.

Scythe (3 hrs) - A digital adaptation of the strategy boardgame with the same name. In an alternative history (mechs!), alternative geography 1920’s, various nations struggle over territory and resources. Seems like a fairly faithful repoduction of the game and tabletop experience. Probably only worthwhile if you are already know and are interested in the boardgame.

Spin Hero (3 hrs) - Slot machine fantasy roguelike - like a deckbuilder, but instead of building a deck of cards you collect symbols that are on the slot machine. Each spin is a turn of combat where the symbols apply verious combo effects. The problem is there is not much to do once the symbols are selected - either the symbols come up or they don’t. Battles only take a few minutes, but that is really dead time without interesting decisions. Also nice-to-have UI things also seemed to have been overlooked - like a tutorial or some tooltips. A nice idea that doesn’t work for me.

Silent Age (1 hr) - Point and click puzzle adventure telling a linear time-travel story. Like most of this games, my interest waned quickly and I just started clicking and combing everything. Not my thing.
entry.summary: Games played since the start of 2025…

entry.title: Dwellingup
entry.content:
Over my birthday I made a weekend trip down to Dwellingup at fairly short notice. The days were spend hiking in the local Jarrah forest, and the nights spent collapsing after walking for hours. There are not enough photos for a slideshow, so I have just put a few below along with some notes. It was a pleasant weekend, and a good reminder that such places can be close to the city. Perhaps I should head out to them more often.

  • The weather was cooler than usual and perfect for hiking: warm but not hot. Long may this continue (although the forecast says the traditional blazing WA summer is about to hit soon). This meant we could appreciate the beauty of the forest rather than feel like we were on a forced march before inevitably melting in the sun.
  • For the first time in a while, the flies were annoying (no mozzies though).
  • There appears to be a single restaurant in Dwellingup open for dinner, and by restaurant I mean pub, and by dinner I mean the kitchen shuts at 7:15pm. It was standard WA country pub menu at the standard quality, ok but nothing special. For the second night we drove down to Pinjarrah (just a short 20 min away) and had a surprisingly good curry.
  • Most of the hiking paths were easy to follow (many were shared with the Munda Biddi Trail), but for while there was just a vaguely cleared track through the bush. Inevitably we got lost and added a few kilometers before getting back on course. We also saw many fallen trail markers laying in the ground (maybe one we didn’t see was the cause of the detour). I should probably invest in some non-phone network navigation device, because this keeps happening.

entry.title: Bunbury
entry.content:
A couple of weeks after travelling to Sri Lanka, I went a few hours south to spend a long weekend in Bunbury and its surrounds. It is amazing how it becomes noticeably cooler and greener with such a short journey. Walking around Bunbury is easy and pretty, although you are finished quickly since the town is surprisingly small. There is one main street, a couple of malls and a few streets full of big box stores. Restaurant selection is limited. The farmers market is still a great food-only supermarket. Prices seemed largely the same as Perth. Overall it felt like a large successful country town, which I suppose it is.

Other places visited:

  • The Donnybrook Apple Festival is very popular, it felt like there were thousands of visitors taking over this small town! And it does not seem to have much to do with apples - there was just a single stall selling apples (very tasty!) and few others selling “related” products. The event seems like a cross between a small agricultural show and and a large standard market.
  • Australind felt like a commuter suburb. There was a nice Italian restaurant though (forgotten its name).
  • Busselton has become a tourist town. Despite being much smaller, the main shopping street was nearly as large as Bunbury’s. However, the shops there felt like they were mostly for visitors.

Some photos from the trip are in a short slideshow available here.

entry.title: Sri Lanka
entry.content:
At the star of April I spent a fortnight in Sri Lanka for a wedding. Perhaps half the time was spent on travelling (see below) and the wedding activities, but we managed some sightseeing along the way. Overall it seems like a nice place to visit, although I’m in no rush to go back (despite missing some good stuff like Sigiriya). People have said it is similar to the Bali of 30 years ago. I can see that, it seems to be a good place to relax by the beach. Some thoughts:

  • There are surprisingly few restaurants everywhere we went (except the Negombo tourist strip). We probably only had 3 meals at local eateries, and that took some effort. I thought perhaps they were there, but I wasn’t looking for the right signs. However, I checked with various online maps, then confirmed by talking to locals and other tourists. Apparently Sri Lankans don’t tend to eat out often and tourists spend most of their time at touristy places (so outside those places good luck!).
  • Colombo is jarring mix of run down building and new towers, often very close to eachother.
  • You are dangerously gem deficient! Walking around the capital we were regularly approached by initially friendly men who quickly told us that we were lucky to be in town that day as there was a special one-day only sale at the best gem store in town. We must go! This was over many different days and stores. One was a little aggressive, but all eventually accepted we weren’t going anywhere with them.
  • Expect to pay more as a non-local, sometimes by a lot. For example, when a taxi wanted more from us than a equivalent Australian taxi (which are not cheap) we tried Uber and got a car at tenth of the asking price.
  • Security sometimes can be very tight, other times non-existent. Going into hotels and shopping malls we went through metal detectors and bag checks. However, other places like train stations had no security, often not even a ticket check. There was no visible security on the streets either (although it still felt safe). Presumably this is a holdover from the long finished civil war and more recent protests.
  • The train network is extensive and amazingly cheap, but incredibly slow and often delayed. Don’t be overly concerned about going in the lower classes as long as you have a set seat. We went in reserved 3rd class for one trip - it was fine and was not that much worse than 1st (no A/C, but we had the windows open). Overall we spent two nearly entire days travelling a few hundred kilometers and back again.
  • The surrounds of Hatton are pretty (not so much the town itself), but there is not much else. The main site seems to be Adam’s Peak a sacred site at the top of a mountain and the destination for a lot of internal tourism. It is extremely busy!
  • Negombo has a strip along the beach full of bars, restaurants, hotels, and shops of local arts. It seemed pleasant but definitely tourist focused. We had a very good fish meal there in a restaurant just off the strip on our last night.
  • It was hard to find good flights to Sri Lanka. Avoiding budget airlines and overly long flights meant we had two options. Both arrived and departed near midnight. Relatively cheap though.

Some photos from the trip are in a short slideshow available here.
